section.title: Blessed Is the Forgiven
section.sectionRationale: A maskil, a wisdom psalm of David, opening with the blessedness of forgiven sin, later quoted by Paul in Romans 4:6-8 as Old Testament testimony to justification by faith apart from works. David recalls the physical anguish of unconfessed sin, the relief of honest confession, and closes urging others not to resist God's instruction like a stubborn animal but to trust and rejoice.
section.thesis: David's testimony that blessedness belongs to the one whose transgression is forgiven and whose sin the LORD does not count against him becomes, in Paul's hands, a foundational Old Testament witness that righteousness before God is received by faith, not earned by works.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the blessedness of forgiven sin (1-2); the anguish of unconfessed sin (3-4); confession, forgiveness, and refuge (5-7); instruction not to be stubborn like a horse or mule (8-9); and a closing contrast between the wicked and the trusting, ending in rejoicing (10-11).

units.label: Blessed is he whose transgressions are forgiven

verses.text: Blessed is he whose {{pesha|transgressions}} are forgiven, whose sin is {{kacah|covered}}.

Blessed is the man whose iniquity the LORD does not count against him, 
in whose spirit there is no deceit.
When I kept silent, my bones became brittle from my groaning all day long.
For day and night Your hand was heavy upon me; my strength was drained as in the summer heat. Selah

units.label: I acknowledged my sin to You

verses.text: Then I {{yadah|acknowledged}} my sin to You and did not hide my iniquity. I said, "I will confess my transgressions to the LORD," and You forgave the guilt of my sin. Selah
Therefore let all the godly pray to You while You may be found. Surely when great waters rise, they will not come near.

You are my hiding place. You protect me from trouble; 
You surround me with songs of deliverance. Selah

units.label: Do not be like the horse or mule

verses.text: I will instruct you and teach you the way you should go; I will give you counsel and watch over you.
Do not be like the horse or mule, which have no understanding; they must be controlled with bit and bridle to make them come to you.

units.label: Be glad in the LORD and rejoice

verses.text: Many are the sorrows of the wicked, but loving devotion surrounds him who trusts in the LORD.
Be glad in the LORD and rejoice, O righteous ones; shout for joy, all you upright in heart.

pesha.gloss: Transgression, willful rebellion against a known standard, more serious than a mere mistake. That such rebellion can be forgiven, not merely excused, is the psalm's opening wonder, later cited by Paul as evidence of justification by faith, Romans 4:7.

kacah.gloss: To cover, conceal. God Himself covers the sin He forgives, not hiding it from His own knowledge but removing it from account against the sinner, a picture developed fully in the atoning covering Christ provides.

yadah.gloss: To confess, acknowledge, give thanks, from a root meaning to throw or cast, as in casting off pretense. David's decisive turn from silence to open acknowledgment of sin is the hinge on which the whole psalm turns from anguish to relief.

basic.context: David opens with the blessedness of the one whose transgression is forgiven and whose sin the LORD does not count against him. He recalls the physical anguish, bones wasting, strength drained, that came from keeping silent about his sin, until he acknowledged it openly and received forgiveness. He urges all the godly to pray while God may be found, celebrates God as his hiding place, and closes with instruction not to be stubborn like an unthinking animal, but to trust the LORD and rejoice.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm should be read as personal testimony turned into general wisdom instruction: David's own experience of hidden guilt and open confession becomes a pattern offered to 'all the godly,' verse 6, and its opening verses become, in the New Testament, a foundational text for understanding forgiveness as God's gift rather than a human achievement.
basic.originalLanguages: David's pesha, willful transgression, is not merely excused but kacah, covered, by God's own action, and the psalm turns entirely on David's yadah, open acknowledgment of sin, moving from destructive silence to relief and song.
basic.typology: David's testimony that the LORD does not count iniquity against the one He forgives, verse 2, anticipates the full reckoning of righteousness apart from works that Paul finds fulfilled in Christ, in whom believers are counted righteous by faith, Romans 4:6-8, 2 Corinthians 5:21.
basic.christ: Paul quotes Psalm 32:1-2 directly in Romans 4:6-8 as Old Testament proof that God has always counted righteousness to sinners apart from works, a reality fulfilled completely in Jesus Christ, who bears the guilt David's confession removes and in whom God does not count our transgressions against us, 2 Corinthians 5:19, 21. David's hiding place, verse 7, anticipates Christ Himself, in whom believers take refuge from every accusation and every flood of trouble.
basic.god: God is shown as one whose hand is heavy on unconfessed sin, not out of cruelty but to draw the sinner toward honest confession, and who forgives completely and immediately the moment sin is acknowledged, becoming a hiding place and surrounding the trusting with songs of deliverance.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 4:6-8 quotes this psalm directly as proof that righteousness comes by faith, not works, the foundational New Testament use of this text. 2 Corinthians 5:21 shows Christ made sin for us so that we might become the righteousness of God, the ultimate fulfillment of not having sin counted against us. 1 John 1:9 echoes this psalm's pattern, that confessing sin brings God's faithful and just forgiveness.
basic.oneStory: David's testimony that blessedness belongs to the one whose transgression is forgiven and whose sin is not counted against him becomes, through Paul's use of this very psalm, a foundational witness to the gospel: that in Jesus Christ, sinners are counted righteous by faith, their guilt covered fully and finally by His atoning work.

context.literary:
The psalm has a clear four part plan, and the parts are marked by the speaker's changing posture. Verses 1 and 2 are a beatitude spoken to the world, in the third person. Verses 3 to 5 are testimony in the first person, addressed to God. Verses 6 and 7 turn back to the community with a 'therefore' and then to God again with 'You are my hiding place'. Verses 8 to 11 are instruction, in which a teacher's voice speaks in the second person, ending with a call to joy. The poem begins by talking about a blessed person, moves to talk with God, and ends by talking to other people, which is the movement of a confession that becomes a lesson.

The word Selah, a pause or lift of some kind in the singing, marks the hinges. It stands after verse 4, verse 5 and verse 7, and each time it falls at a change of mood: after the heavy hand, after the forgiveness, and after the song of deliverance. The reader is being asked to pause where the psalm turns.

The opening is built by a strict piling up of parallels. Verses 1 and 2 give three words for wrongdoing and three for God's answer, and verse 5 repeats the whole set as David's experience: three words for what he did, three verbs for what he did or refused to do, and forgiveness at the end. The doctrine is stated first and then lived, and the psalm's shape says that the doctrine of verses 1 and 2 is the account of what happened to a man.

The heading calls the poem a maskil. The word is related to the Hebrew verb for giving insight, and the psalm uses that verb itself in verse 8, 'I will instruct you'. The label is not decoration, since the psalm sets out to teach. Its lesson closes with the contrast of the horse and mule against the understanding person, and with the difference between the sorrows of the wicked and the loving devotion that surrounds the trusting, verse 10. The last verse invites a shout of joy, so that a psalm which begins in silence ends in noise.
context.historical:
Tradition ties the psalm to David's sin with Bathsheba and Uriah, 2 Samuel 11, and to the visit of Nathan, 2 Samuel 12, when David said, 'I have sinned against the LORD', and Nathan replied, 'The LORD has taken away your sin', 2 Samuel 12:13. Psalm 51 has a heading that says so explicitly, and Psalm 32 is its companion. The heading of this psalm does not name the occasion, and the link is a reasonable inference from the shared vocabulary and the mention of a period of silence. What the text makes plain is that David knew the experience of an unconfessed sin that wore him down, and the memory of it shaped his teaching.

The physical descriptions in verses 3 and 4 correspond to the way Israel thought of a person as a unity. Sin was not only a matter of the mind, and guilt could be felt in the bones, in strength and in appetite. The heat of summer is a picture Israelites knew well, since the dry season took the moisture out of the land. The 'hand' of the LORD in verse 4 is the hand of judgment known in 1 Samuel 5:6, where it lay heavy on Ashdod, and the psalm uses the phrase of discipline rather than of destruction.

The psalm's advice to pray 'while You may be found' echoes the call in Isaiah 55:6, and reflects the belief that there is a time of grace which should not be squandered. The flood of 'great waters' is a familiar picture of overwhelming trouble, and it would remind hearers of the flood story and of the deep waters of Psalm 69:1-2.

The comparison to horse and mule in verse 9 belongs to a culture where animals were controlled by the bit in the mouth. The picture is precise and not a general insult: the animal has no understanding, so it must be forced, and David does not want to be moved that way. The church later counted this psalm among the seven penitential psalms, a set of prayers for the person coming to God in repentance.
context.canonical:
The psalm's first word, 'Blessed', is the word that opens the whole Psalter, Psalm 1:1. That psalm blesses the man who does not walk with the wicked, and this one blesses the man who has been forgiven. The two beatitudes belong side by side, since the person who walks blamelessly and the person who is forgiven are both, in the end, people who have been kept by God. The next psalm continues with 'Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD', Psalm 33:12, and the beatitudes run through the neighbouring psalms.

The three words for sin come from the great self-revelation of Sinai, where the LORD is described as 'forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin', Exodus 34:7. The Day of Atonement uses the same three, when the high priest confesses over the goat 'all the iniquities and rebellious acts of the Israelites in regard to all their sins', Leviticus 16:21, and the goat carries them into the wilderness, Leviticus 16:22. Psalm 85:2 puts two of the verbs of verse 1 side by side: 'You forgave the iniquity of Your people; You covered all their sin.' David's testimony is thus the personal side of what the sacrificial system enacted for the nation.

The psalm's counsel to confess is the doctrine of Proverbs 28:13, 'He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy'. Psalm 51:9 asks God to hide His face from the sins, as though covering were God's business alone, and Micah 7:18 asks who is a God who pardons iniquity.

The New Testament makes the psalm a cornerstone. Paul quotes verses 1 and 2 in Romans 4:6-8 to show that David speaks of a righteousness credited apart from works. John gives the pattern of confession and forgiveness in 1 John 1:8-9, and James connects it with prayer and healing, James 5:16. The sentence 'the LORD does not count' is picked up in 2 Corinthians 5:19, where God is reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, 'not counting men's trespasses against them'.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David wanted his hearers to avoid the mistake he made and to find the way out that he found. The psalm describes a man who thought he could manage his guilt by silence, and who found that silence was not neutral: it consumed him. He wants the godly to know this before they learn it the hard way, and that is why he speaks directly in verse 6, 'Therefore let all the godly pray to You while You may be found.' The godly, in his mind, are not people who have no sin but people who pray about it.

He is also correcting a picture of God. The hand that was heavy in verse 4 is not the hand of an enemy but of a teacher who will not leave a pupil alone in his hiding. When David speaks of the horse and the mule, he wants the reader to choose the way of understanding, to come to God before the bit and bridle are needed. The good news of the psalm is that the way of understanding is open at any time, and that forgiveness is not a reward for a long penance but a gift that follows the honest word.

The closing verses give the reason for the whole poem: the wicked have many sorrows, but loving devotion surrounds the one who trusts, and so the psalm ends in gladness. David wants the reader to be surprised by joy, because joy is the last thing a person expects to find on the far side of confession.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm reports David's own case, and it is careful about cause and effect. It does not say that every illness is caused by hidden sin. Job's friends went wrong at exactly this point, and the Gospels record Jesus rejecting the assumption in John 9:2-3. David is describing what happened to him when he kept silent about a specific wrong, and reading it as a rule for diagnosing anyone else's suffering would turn testimony into accusation.

The psalm's commands are plain, though. The godly are to pray, and verse 8 offers instruction to anyone who will accept it, and verse 9 tells the reader not to be stubborn. There are two points of prescription. The first is that concealed sin harms, and confession is the way out, a truth that James and John repeat, James 5:16 and 1 John 1:9. The second is that forgiveness is described as a gift: covered, lifted, not counted. The psalm does not tell believers to earn their way back. It describes how forgiveness arrives and tells them to receive it and rejoice, verse 11.

debates.question: Who speaks in verses 8 and 9?

views.label: God speaks
views.case: The verses say, 'I will instruct you and teach you the way you should go; I will give you counsel and watch over you.' Many take this as an answer of God to David's confession, an oracle in the middle of the psalm, so that the forgiven man hears the voice of the one who forgave him. The promise 'watch over you' fits the language of divine care.

views.label: David speaks as a teacher
views.case: Others hear David's own voice, since he has just turned to address the godly in verse 6 and the psalm is a maskil, a teaching poem. The advice about the horse and the mule sounds like a wise man's counsel, and the shift from 'You' addressed to God to 'you' addressed to a hearer can be read as a shift of audience.

views.label: Both, since God teaches through the psalm
views.case: Whoever the speaker is, the content is God's own instruction, and the psalm passes from one voice to another without marking the change. It is at home in a book where prophets and psalmists often let God's voice break into a prayer.

debates.bearing: The lesson does not depend on the decision. Either God says He will instruct, or David says God's instruction is available to those who will hear it. In both cases the forgiven person is now a pupil, and his guidance has begun.

debates.question: Does 'no deceit' in verse 2 name a condition for forgiveness or a result of it?

views.label: A result of forgiveness
views.case: Paul quotes verses 1 and 2 to prove that righteousness is credited apart from works, Romans 4:6-8, and the psalm's own story has David sinning first, hiding, and then being forgiven when he stops hiding. The 'no deceit' is the transparency of the person who no longer needs to cover himself.

views.label: A description of the honest confession itself
views.case: The line describes the sort of person who comes to God without pretence. The man who acknowledges his sin has no deceit in his spirit at the point of confessing. Forgiveness is offered to the person who stops lying, but the stopping is not a merit that earns it.

views.label: A condition to be met, in the sense of sincere repentance
views.case: Some read it as a requirement that repentance be genuine, and point to the hypocrisy that God rejects in the prophets. The psalm may then be warning against a confession that is only a performance.

debates.bearing: The first two views respect the way Paul uses the psalm, and the third guards against a hollow confession. The psalm's plain point is that the blessed person is one who has ceased to hide, and that the blessing is God's gift, not a wage.

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm names three kinds of wrongdoing, and it is worth seeing them all together. Beside transgression, which is rebellion against a rightful authority, there is chatta'ah, sin, a word whose root means to miss a mark, and avon, iniquity, a word often linked with the idea of something bent, and used also of the guilt that results. These three occur together in the self-revelation of Exodus 34:7 and the Day of Atonement ritual of Leviticus 16:21. The psalm gathers every kind of failing, rebellion, missing the mark and perversity, and says that God deals with all of them.

The verbs of God's dealing are equally important. In verse 1 the person is one whose transgression is 'forgiven', which is the passive of nasa, to lift or carry. It is the ordinary verb for bearing a load, and it is the verb of Leviticus 16:22, where the goat 'will carry on itself all their iniquities', and of Isaiah 53:12, where the servant 'bore the sin of many'. Forgiveness in this psalm has a weight, because someone must carry the load that is lifted off the sinner. The second verb is kasah, to cover, and the pairing with nasa appears again in Psalm 85:2.

The word 'count' in verse 2 is chashav, to reckon or account. It is the word used of Abram in Genesis 15:6, where his faith was 'credited to him as righteousness'. The Greek Old Testament renders it with logizomai, and Paul draws on that link in Romans 4, setting the credit of Genesis 15:6 beside the non-credit of Psalm 32:2. Paul's argument rests on a real verbal chain: the same verb is used of righteousness that is credited and of sin that is not.

The word for 'deceit' in verse 2 is remiyyah, a word for slackness or treachery, used elsewhere of a false or slack bow. It describes a spirit that does not work straight.

A neat point of grammar arises in verse 5. In verse 1 God is said to have covered the sin. In verse 5 David says he 'did not hide' his iniquity, and the verb is the same one, kasah. The psalm sets human covering against divine covering: the man who covers his own sin remains exposed, and the man who stops covering it has it covered by God. Verse 5 then uses nasa again for God's answer, 'You forgave the guilt of my sin', which returns to the verb of verse 1.

The 'groaning' of verse 3 is a word for a roar, as a lion's, and the picture is of a man whose anguished cries went up day after day. The 'heavy' hand of verse 4 uses the verb kaved, the same root as glory or weight, in a phrase used of the LORD's hand in 1 Samuel 5:6. The 'summer heat' is a picture of the dryness of the Israelite summer, and the BSB footnote notes that a phrase in the line may also be read 'my vitality was turned'.

In verse 7 God 'surrounds' David with songs, and the verb is sabab, which returns in verse 10, where loving devotion 'surrounds' the one who trusts. The circling of songs and the circling of chesed form a pair. In verse 8 the verb 'instruct' is from the same root as maskil in the heading. The Hebrew of verse 9 is famously hard, but the sense of the animal that must be restrained is clear.

typology.type: The bearing away of sin, verse 1
typology.fulfillment: The verb for forgiveness in verse 1 means to lift and carry, and Israel saw the pattern on the Day of Atonement, when the goat carried the nation's iniquities into the wilderness, Leviticus 16:21-22. Isaiah's servant 'bore the sin of many', Isaiah 53:12, and the Baptist points to Jesus as the Lamb of God 'who takes away the sin of the world', John 1:29. Hebrews says Christ 'was offered once to bear the sins of many', Hebrews 9:28. The escalation is that the load was carried by a person and not by an animal, and it was carried once for all. The goat's journey needed repeating every year, and the type is fulfilled in a sacrifice that does not need to be offered again.

typology.type: Righteousness credited apart from works, verse 2
typology.fulfillment: Paul takes David's 'blessed is the man whose sin the Lord will never count against him' as proof that God has always credited righteousness apart from works, Romans 4:6-8. He grounds it in Abraham, whose faith was credited as righteousness, Genesis 15:6. The correspondence is the reckoning of God: sin is not counted, righteousness is. In Christ the reckoning is possible because He 'was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification', Romans 4:25. The type falls short in that David's forgiveness, in the psalm, looks forward to a payment not yet made. In Christ, God is shown 'to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus', Romans 3:26.

David calls the LORD his hiding place. Paul says of believers, 'your life is now hidden with Christ in God', Colossians 3:3, and the way to shelter in God's presence has been opened through Christ's body, Hebrews 10:19-20. In the psalm the hiding place shelters a forgiven man from the floods of trouble, verse 6. In Christ it shelters a believer from the accusation itself, since 'there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus', Romans 8:1. The type is limited in that David's hiding place shielded him within this life, while the shelter in Christ reaches through death.

typology.type: The horse and mule, and the guidance of the Spirit, verses 8 and 9
typology.fulfillment: David is told not to be led by force like an animal, but to be taught with counsel and watchful care. In the new covenant this is promised as an inward teaching. Jeremiah spoke of a law written on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33, and Jesus told His disciples that the Spirit would guide them into all the truth, John 16:13. The correspondence is between a God who instructs and a people who respond willingly. The type is exceeded because, under the new covenant, the willing heart is itself a gift of God.

study.christ:
The psalm points to Christ first through its central language of forgiveness as bearing. David says that his transgression is lifted and his sin covered, and that the LORD does not count iniquity against him. In the Old Testament, lifting a load is the work of a substitute: the scapegoat carried iniquities away, Leviticus 16:22, and the servant of Isaiah 53 bore the sin of many, Isaiah 53:12. The New Testament says Jesus is that servant. He 'bore our sins in His body on the tree', to use Peter's summary in 1 Peter 2:24, and John the Baptist's phrase 'takes away', John 1:29, points the same way. The heavy hand of verse 4 is lifted from David because it was, in the plan of God, laid on another. Isaiah says, 'the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all', Isaiah 53:6.

The second link is the Lord's refusal to count. Paul quotes verse 2 in Romans 4:8 and returns to it in 2 Corinthians 5:19, where God, in Christ, is 'not counting men's trespasses against them'. He then gives the mechanism two verses later: 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God', 2 Corinthians 5:21. The sin is not ignored. It is counted, and counted against Christ. The forgiven person of the psalm stands blessed because the debt has been dealt with. Colossians says it was 'canceled' and nailed to the cross, Colossians 2:13-14.

Third, Christ is the advocate that the confessing sinner can trust. John writes that anyone who does sin has 'an advocate before the Father, Jesus Christ, the Righteous One', and that He is the atoning sacrifice, 1 John 2:1-2. The invitation of verse 5 to acknowledge sin openly is answered by the fact that the God who receives the confession has already provided the means of forgiveness. He is 'faithful and just to forgive', 1 John 1:9, which is another way of saying that forgiveness in Christ does not compromise God's righteousness but displays it, Romans 3:25-26.

The hiding place of verse 7 points to Christ in the same way. The one who cried 'why have You forsaken Me' bore the floods, so that those who take shelter in Him need not. The 'songs of deliverance' that surround David are the songs of a people redeemed, and the last verse's call to shout for joy has its fullest voice in the worship of the Lamb.

There are limits to this reading. David's own experience was that of a sinner, and nothing in the psalm is put on Jesus' lips. The link is not that Christ prays the psalm, but that the psalm describes the blessing which Christ's work makes available, and that the New Testament itself uses it that way. The New Testament authors treat David as one who saw, in the shadow of the sacrificial system, the shape of a forgiveness that would be completed on the cross.
study.god:
This psalm shows a God who is not indifferent to sin, and also not eager to punish. The hand of verse 4 is heavy by day and by night, and the psalm does not hide the fact that God's dealings with a hidden sin are severe. But the point of the heaviness is plain from what follows: as soon as David speaks, the weight lifts. The God of the psalm presses on a wound to get the poison out, and He does not press for its own sake.

He is a God who forgives at once and completely. There is no interval in verse 5 between 'I will confess' and 'You forgave'. The verse gives no account of a period of probation, and it does not tell of a sacrifice David had to bring first. This does not mean that forgiveness is cheap, since the rest of Scripture shows its cost, Romans 3:25-26. It means that God's readiness is greater than the sinner's expectation, and He is described in Exodus 34:6-7 as 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion'. Micah wonders at a God who 'pardons iniquity and passes over the transgression', Micah 7:18.

He is a God who reckons. The verb of verse 2 gives God an account book, and the question is whether sin is entered against a person. The psalm presents God as free to decide not to count, and Paul insists that He does this justly, Romans 3:26. He does not pretend that sin is small. He deals with it, and then declines to hold it against the forgiven.

He is a God who covers and hides, in a good sense. The word for covering that David refused to do for himself is the word God does for him. The Lord is a hiding place, seter, a place from which the trouble outside cannot reach in. In a psalm about the danger of hiding from God, the last word is that the safest place to hide is in Him.

He is a teacher who prefers understanding to force. Verses 8 and 9 show a God who would rather instruct than use the bit and bridle. It is a striking description of divine guidance: counsel given with His eye on the pupil, and a plain wish that the people should come to Him freely. Where they will not, He is capable of using the heavy hand, but that is not His first wish.

He is a God who sings over His people. The 'songs of deliverance' that surround David in verse 7 are echoed in Zephaniah 3:17, where the LORD 'will rejoice over you with singing'. In the psalm, God is the one who surrounds the forgiven man with joy.

For worship, the psalm shows what it is to bring the truth about ourselves to God without hiding, and it puts on the believer's lips a thanksgiving that begins with 'Blessed'. It teaches a congregation to be a community where confession is safe, because the God who hears it is the God who forgives.

crossReferences.note: Paul quotes verses 1 and 2 as David's testimony that God credits righteousness apart from works. He sets it beside Abraham's faith, Genesis 15:6, and shows that the two texts share one verb, so that the reckoning of righteousness and the non-reckoning of sin are the same act of grace. It is the New Testament's most direct use of the psalm.

The LORD declares Himself compassionate, gracious and slow to anger, forgiving iniquity, transgression and sin. Psalm 32 uses these three words and shows the promise coming true in a single life. David's confession is the experience of the divine name, and the psalm gives the general revelation its personal application.

On the Day of Atonement the high priest confesses the iniquities, rebellious acts and sins of Israel over the goat, and the goat carries them away into the wilderness. The three words and the verb of carrying match verses 1 and 5, so that the psalm's teaching is the inward side of the outward ritual.

The psalmist says that God forgave the iniquity of His people and covered all their sin. It uses the same pair of verbs as verse 1 and applies them to the nation, showing that David's personal experience matches what Israel knew corporately of the LORD's mercy.

Nathan confronts David and David says, 'I have sinned against the LORD.' Nathan answers that the LORD has taken away his sin. The exchange shows how brief the confession was and how prompt the pardon, matching verse 5. It is the narrative that many readers take as the background to the psalm.

The one who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy. It summarises the wisdom of verses 3 to 5 in a single proverb, and it shows that David's testimony was consistent with the older teaching of the wise, which the psalm turns into experience.

The prophet urges his hearers to seek the LORD while He may be found and to call on Him while He is near. The phrase matches verse 6, and both texts treat access to God as an opportunity to be taken. Together they urge the reader not to postpone honesty with God.

The servant bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors. The verb for bearing is the verb behind 'forgiven' in verse 1. The connection shows how the forgiveness David enjoyed is founded on the work of the servant, who takes on Himself the load that is lifted from the sinner.

God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, not counting men's trespasses against them, and made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf. Paul's 'not counting' is the psalm's phrase, and verse 21 gives the reason why God can afford not to count: He counted it against His Son.

John says that if we say we have no sin we deceive ourselves, and that if we confess, God is faithful and just to forgive. The pattern is verse 5 in the New Testament: honest confession, and then a forgiveness that is secured by God's own faithfulness. It shows the psalm's teaching continuing in the life of the church.

James tells believers to confess their sins to each other and pray for each other so that they may be healed. It applies the psalm's discovery, that hidden guilt sickens and open confession heals, to the life of a community, and it makes confession a shared practice and not only a private one.

The next psalm opens with a call to rejoice in the LORD, O righteous ones, which echoes the last verse of this one. The two psalms are neighbours, and the joy at the end of Psalm 32 becomes the song of Psalm 33. The forgiven person is brought into the worshipping congregation.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible begins with a couple who covered themselves and hid, Genesis 3:7-8, and the first act of God after their sin was to call, 'Where are you?' Psalm 32 is the story of one person who did the same thing and then found a better way. He kept silent, and his strength drained away. When he ceased covering his sin and told the truth, God covered it. In that pattern the psalm answers the question that hangs over the opening chapters: what can a person do who has sinned and cannot undo it?

The answer runs through the story of Israel. God named Himself to Moses as the one who forgives iniquity, transgression and sin, Exodus 34:7, and He gave His people a tabernacle and a day of atonement in which the carrying away of sin was acted out, Leviticus 16. The prophets kept alive the hope that God would deal with sin at its root, Micah 7:18-19. Yet the system pointed beyond itself, since animals could not finally take away sins, Hebrews 10:4. David's blessing is real, but it awaits a sacrifice that is sufficient.

That sacrifice is Christ. In Him the one who lifts and carries the sin of many is found, and the crediting of righteousness is possible without any pretence that the sin was small. Paul reads this psalm as showing that the gospel was not a late idea, since David already lived by grace. Abraham believed and was credited righteousness; David was forgiven without works; and the church now stands in the same line. The line stretches back and forward, and every believer is a version of David at the point of confessing.

In the new creation there is nothing left to hide. The people of God will see His face, and the book of Revelation says that the accuser has been thrown down, Revelation 12:10. The conscience that made David's bones brittle will be clean. The songs of deliverance that surrounded him in a single moment surround the whole redeemed company, and the call to shout for joy, all you upright in heart, is finally answered by a people who no longer have to remember the silence.

sermon.title: Confession and Forgiveness
sermon.why: Begg preaches directly through Psalm 32, teaching that confessing sin before the Lord ultimately leads to joy, and that the psalmist's experience of concealed guilt giving way to confessed relief models the pattern every believer needs.

quiz.q: What does David say in verses 1-2 that Paul later quotes directly in Romans 4:6-8?

options.text: Blessed is the one whose transgressions are forgiven and whose iniquity the LORD does not count against him.
options.note: Paul uses this exact testimony as Old Testament evidence for righteousness reckoned by faith apart from works.

options.text: Blessed is the one who feels no guilt over sin.
options.note: Close, since relief from guilt is part of the picture, but the blessing specifically rests on being forgiven and not counted guilty by God, not merely on an absence of felt guilt.

options.text: Blessed is the one who offers the most sacrifices.
options.note: The psalm's blessing concerns forgiveness of sin, not the quantity of ritual sacrifice.

options.text: Blessed is the one who hides his sin well.
options.note: The psalm's larger point, verses 3-5, is that hiding sin brings anguish, while confession brings relief.

quiz.q: What happened to David physically while he kept silent about his sin, according to verses 3-4?

options.text: His bones became brittle from groaning, and his strength was drained as in summer heat.
options.note: David describes real physical anguish resulting from unconfessed, concealed sin.

options.text: He felt only mild, occasional discomfort of conscience.
options.note: Close, since some inner discomfort is implied, but the text describes severe, continuous anguish, bones wasting and strength drained, not mild or occasional discomfort.

options.text: He grew stronger the longer he concealed his sin.
options.note: This is the opposite of the described experience, wasting strength, not increased strength.

options.text: He lost his position as king.
options.note: The described effects are physical and internal, not political loss of position.

quiz.q: What changed for David in verse 5?

options.text: He acknowledged his sin and did not hide his iniquity, and God forgave the guilt of his sin.
options.note: This verse marks the psalm's turning point from concealment to confession and immediate forgiveness.

options.text: He simply resolved internally to do better in the future.
options.note: Close, since a change of heart is involved, but verse 5 specifically describes spoken confession to God, not a private resolution to improve.

options.text: He blamed others for his sin.
options.note: Verse 5 describes David taking personal responsibility, not shifting blame.

options.text: He continued to hide his sin but felt better anyway.
options.note: The text specifically says he stopped hiding his iniquity; concealment did not continue.

quiz.q: What warning does David give in verse 9?

options.text: Do not be like the horse or mule, which must be controlled with bit and bridle because they lack understanding.
options.note: David warns against stubborn resistance to God's instruction, unlike an unthinking animal that must be forced.

options.text: Do not rely on animals for daily transportation.
options.note: Close, since horses and mules are named, but the point of the warning is stubborn resistance to God's guidance, illustrated by these animals, not a rule about transportation.

options.text: Do not trust in wealth or possessions.
options.note: While related to trust, the specific image in verse 9 is about stubborn resistance to guidance, not wealth.

options.text: Do not seek God's counsel at all.
options.note: This is the opposite; verse 8 promises God's instruction and counsel, and verse 9 warns against resisting it.

quiz.q: How does the psalm close in verses 10-11?

options.text: Contrasting the many sorrows of the wicked with those surrounded by loving devotion, calling the righteous to rejoice.
options.note: The psalm ends by drawing a clear contrast and issuing a joyful call to worship.

options.text: With a general statement that life is difficult for everyone equally.
options.note: Close, since sorrow is mentioned, but the text draws a specific contrast between the many sorrows of the wicked and the loving devotion surrounding the one who trusts the LORD, not an equal difficulty for all.

options.text: With David returning to silence about his sin.
options.note: The psalm closes in joyful praise, not a return to silence.

options.text: With a warning that even the righteous cannot be forgiven.
options.note: The psalm's whole message is the opposite, that forgiveness is available and leads to rejoicing for the righteous.

questions: David describes physical anguish, wasting bones and drained strength, from concealing his sin. Have you ever experienced the toll of hiding sin instead of confessing it, and what finally moved you toward honesty?

Paul uses this psalm to teach that righteousness comes by faith, not works. Do you tend to relate to God more on the basis of your performance or on the basis of Christ's righteousness credited to you?
David says God instructs and counsels those who do not resist Him like a stubborn animal. Where in your life are you currently resisting God's clear counsel rather than yielding to it?

David calls the LORD his hiding place, surrounding him with songs of deliverance rather than accusation. Where do you need to run to God as refuge this week instead of facing trouble in your own strength?

The psalm closes urging the righteous to rejoice and shout for joy. Does your own experience of forgiveness produce this kind of joy, or has forgiveness become something you take for granted rather than celebrate?

translationNotes.note: Covered renders kacah, the same root behind the Day of Atonement's kapporet, the mercy seat, both pointing to sin dealt with by God's own covering action rather than human effort.
Acknowledged renders yadah, related to a root for casting off or throwing, picturing confession as decisively casting off pretense rather than merely admitting a fact.
Bit and bridle were tools used to force unwilling animals into compliance, a vivid contrast to the willing, understanding obedience the LORD desires from His people.
